title: A host's corpus map -- what each PLACE holds, and how high a resident of it may reach (ADR-019 decision 1)
description: The second and last of the two sites from which an artifact's class and authority may be read; the first is the artifact's own front matter. A host writes `.agents/project/corpus/*.json` -- one file or several, each an independent set of rows, merged by path -- and states in TENS of rows what its THOUSANDS of documents are made of. Modelled row-for-row on the records map (`layout` schema): every field an entry there already has means the same thing here and is spelled the same way, because a second word for one truth is the drift this ADR exists to stop. Two properties are the whole design. (1) A row may CONFER a class on a place's residents and may NEVER RAISE authority: `authority_ceiling` caps what a resident may declare and supplies nothing, and no word of the vocabulary appears in this schema or in any interpreter (Cardinals II and IV). (2) A row is a DECLARATION a human wrote, reviewable in one diff, with one author -- never an inference from a filename or a path, which is the defect this replaces (Cardinal VII). LAZY: a host that declares no corpus map at all is legal and green. The mechanism exists from the day it ships; the artifact is instantiated the day it has content, and an empty map is the absence of a map, not a row saying nothing.

id.description: What this FILE of the map is, so that a host writing several of them names each one once. A map is merged by path across files; the id is the file's identity and never a place's, and two files claiming one id is refused where every collection's identity is -- a name that resolves to two things is not a name.

summary.description: What this file of the map covers, for a reader deciding whether to open it. Free prose: it binds nothing and is projected nowhere.

places.description: One row per PLACE -- a directory or a single file -- that this host wishes to state something about. Absence of a row is not a defect: an unmapped place holds unclassified artifacts, which is a declared state and is counted, never guessed at.

path.description: Root-relative, POSIX-formed; a directory path ends in '/'. The same spelling rule as the records map, so one reader reads both.

holds.description: The class this place CONFERS on a resident that declares none: the id of one `kinds` row of the record-keeping vocabulary, never a free word. Conferred, not inferred -- a human wrote this row about this place. A resident that declares its own kind keeps it; a resident of no mapped place stays unclassified and is counted as such, and the catalog can tell the three apart.

authority_ceiling.description: The MOST a resident of this place may bind: the id of any `authorities` row. It CAPS and never confers -- an artifact that declares nothing is unclassified here as everywhere, and an artifact that declares more than the ceiling is REFUSED rather than quietly demoted, because a document whose own word and whose place disagree is a contradiction a person must settle. A place may LOWER a claim and may never RAISE one, with no exception at the top: that is how a place where nothing may be current (a history, an archive) demotes a stale claim by location, which is the failure a filename-derived authority produces and this design exists to kill. Absent means the default ceiling -- the vocabulary's ordinary supporting row -- so the most binding state is reachable only where a place says so AND the artifact says so (ADR-019 amendment 1).

owned_by.description: The record this place BELONGS TO -- the collection it lives in, and its id. This is how a unit of work comes to own a place of its own (ADR-020 decision 6): the sentence lives on the ROW, where a place comes into existence at all, and never on the record. The other direction was available and is refused -- a path written on a record is a CLAIM about a file, unchecked where it is written, rotting silently, and reading afterwards exactly like a claim that is still true. Absent means this place belongs to the corpus at large, which is what almost every place is. No class of record and no collection is named by the kit: which collection owns which places is this host's statement about its own tree, and an owner nothing here can resolve is REFUSED rather than ignored, because a place whose owner does not exist outlives the work it was opened for.

collection.description: The name a capability declared this collection readable under (`reads_as`), resolved against what this host has enabled -- never a path.

id.description: The id of the record in that collection. One record may own at most one place here, and one place has at most one owner.

entry.description: Whether this place is a ROOT of the route graph -- one of the few surfaces from which the work is actually steered, and therefore a place every live obligation must be reachable FROM. Absent means false: an entry root is claimed, never assumed, because a graph whose roots are everything has no unreachable nodes and measures nothing.

read_when.description: The retrieval key: the task triggers, in the words a task actually arrives in, that pull this place into context. The same field, spelled the same way, as on a records-map entry -- the navigation projection reads both and invents no `answers` vocabulary of its own. A row without it is legal and simply answers no question.

indexed_by.description: The root-relative path of the artifact that INDEXES this place. Two things follow from one declaration: the place's residents become reachable through it in the route graph, and the index becomes answerable for completeness in both directions -- a resident it omits and a link that resolves to nothing are equally its defect. Absent means the place has no index and none is expected of it.

writer.description: Who may write this place: the id of one `writers` row of the record-keeping vocabulary. Same field and same vocabulary as the records map; projected into the catalog beside the class.

lifecycle.description: How this place's content ages and where it goes: the id of one `lifecycles` row of the record-keeping vocabulary. Same field and same vocabulary as the records map.

budgets.description: One row per corpus-wide invariant this host undertakes to hold, and the whole of what turns the counts above into a VERDICT (ADR-019 decision 9). A budget is a CEILING that may fall in an ordinary edit and may never rise: `FF-CORPUS-RATCHET` refuses a row raised above the value of the previous accepted state, a row that was accepted and is now deleted, and a measured count standing above the ceiling that was meant to cap it. Nothing else. Absent means this host has undertaken nothing -- legal, green, and stated as such rather than reported as a corpus within its budgets. Deliberately NOT a percentage and not a deadline: a ratio improves when its denominator grows, so a corpus could 'improve' by acquiring documents, and a date is not a mechanism because it expires and takes the rule with it.

measures.description: The id of the MEASURE this row caps -- a count published by the module of the kit that already reads it, exactly as a gate kind is answered by the module that judges it. No measure is listed in this schema or in the ratchet: a budget over a count nobody can take is refused at run time with the published names printed, because a closed list here would mean a host could only budget what this file was last edited to know about (Cardinals II and IV).

ceiling.description: The most this host accepts for that measure. An integer and never a rate. Zero is the terminal value: a budget that reaches it matures its gate to `enforce` under ADR-006, and the zero becomes unraisable like every other value -- by the same refusal, with no special case for it. No lower bound is stated here because this kit's schema subset carries no numeric bounds, deliberately (`validation.py`), and a keyword the validator would refuse is worse than none: a ceiling below anything measurable needs no schema to catch it, since the measured count then stands above it and the ratchet refuses on that.

measured.description: The date the number was taken, ISO `YYYY-MM-DD`. Required, because a ceiling is a reading of the world at a moment and a reading whose moment is unstated cannot be told apart from a guess (Cardinal III). It is never checked for freshness -- the measured count is compared with the ceiling on every run, which is a stronger answer than any date could give -- and it is what a reader uses to tell a budget that was measured from a budget that was hoped for.

note.description: Why this host carries this budget, for the reader of the next raise attempt. Free prose: it binds nothing and is projected nowhere.
